name: TPA6203A1DGNR
title: Mono 1.25 W differential-input audio power amplifier
summary: A class-AB mono amplifier with differential inputs and a bridge-tied output, for speakers of 8 Ω and up. It runs from 2.5 V to 5.5 V on 1.7 mA, gives 1.25 W into 8 Ω at 5 V and 1 % THD+N, and needs only five external parts: input coupling and the mid-supply bypass capacitor are optional. Packages are a 2 mm × 2 mm BGA, a 3 mm × 3 mm QFN and an 8-pin PowerPAD MSOP.
key_figures: 1.25 W into 8 Ω at 5 V, THD+N = 1%
-87 dB, 217 Hz to 2 kHz, 3.6 V to 5.5 V
audio passes 4 µs after shutdown release

circuits.title: Differential input from a DAC
circuits.description: A differential source drives IN- and IN+ through the two RI resistors with no coupling capacitors; RF from VO+ back to IN- and from VO- back to IN+ sets the gain at RF/RI, 1 V/V with these values. The speaker sits across VO+ and VO-. CS decouples the battery supply at VDD, the SHUTDOWN line enables the amplifier, and CBYPASS on the mid-supply node may be left off.
notes: Typical values: RI = RF = 10 kΩ, C(BYPASS) = 0.22 µF, CS = 1 µF.

circuits.title: Differential input with input capacitors
circuits.description: The same bridge amplifier as the DAC circuit, with a CI capacitor in series ahead of each RI so the source's DC level is blocked. Each CI with its RI forms a high-pass corner at 1/(2π RI CI).
notes: Typical values: RI = RF = 10 kΩ, C(BYPASS) = 0.22 µF, CS = 1 µF, CI = 0.22 µF.

circuits.title: Single-ended input
circuits.description: A single-ended source enters through CI and RI to IN-. The other RI, on IN+, goes to ground through its own CI, so both inputs see the same impedance. RF from each output back to its input sets the gain at RF/RI; the speaker is across the two outputs.
notes: Typical values: RI = RF = 10 kΩ, C(BYPASS) = 0.22 µF, CS = 1 µF, CI = 0.22 µF.

operation.text: Inside are a differential amplifier, which makes the output difference equal to the input difference times the gain, and a common-mode loop, which holds the average of the two outputs near VDD/2 whatever the common-mode level at the inputs.

Because common-mode rejection is high, the inputs can sit at a DC level other than mid-supply, such as a DAC's lower mid-point, and the outputs still centre on VDD/2. Input coupling capacitors are needed only when the input common-mode level falls outside 0.5 V to VDD − 0.8 V. Without them, use gain resistors of 1 % tolerance or tighter.
A shift of the mid-supply node moves both outputs together and cancels across the load, so C(BYPASS) can be left out. Leaving it out costs a little supply ripple rejection.
GSM handsets pulse their transmitter at 217 Hz, which couples into the input and output wiring; the differential structure rejects it far better than a typical audio amplifier.

RF and RI set the gain and should lie between 1 kΩ and 100 kΩ; most typical curves use RF = RI = 20 kΩ. Output balance about the reference depends on matched resistor ratios: a mismatch degrades CMRR, PSRR and second-harmonic cancellation, so resistors of 1 % or better are recommended.

An internal divider on BYPASS makes the mid-supply voltage for the internal references and fixes the outputs' common-mode level at VDD/2. A capacitor there filters noise and raises kSVR, and also sets how fast VO+ and VO- rise on leaving shutdown: a larger capacitor gives a slower rise. Audio passes 4 µs after shutdown is released, while the gain ramps up at a rate set by C(BYPASS). Start-up time is measured from the rising edge on SHUTDOWN until the gain is within 3 dB of its final value. For least pop, give IN+ and IN- equal source impedance (resistance and capacitance).
SHUTDOWN is active low. With it at 0.8 V or below the supply current is 0.01 µA typical, 0.9 µA maximum, and the outputs are above 10 kΩ; a level of 2 V or more turns the amplifier on.

With a single-ended source, CI is needed to bias the input at the right DC level, and with RI it sets the low-frequency corner. Leakage through RI, CI and RF to the load puts a DC offset at the input that eats headroom, worst at high gain, so a ceramic capacitor is preferred. If a polarised type is used, its positive side normally goes toward the amplifier, whose input sits at VDD/2; check the polarity in each design.

Decoupling keeps THD low and stops oscillation with long speaker leads. A low-ESR ceramic of 0.1 µF to 1 µF as close to VDD as possible handles fast transients; a 10 µF or larger capacitor near the amplifier helps with low-frequency noise but is usually unnecessary given the part's PSRR. Low-ESR capacitors are recommended throughout.

The two outputs drive opposite ends of the speaker, so the swing across it is twice one output's swing and the power four times that of a ground-referenced output from the same supply and load. In a 3.6 V handset into 8 Ω this lifts the limit from 200 mW single-ended to 800 mW, 6 dB more. A single-ended output needs a large coupling capacitor (about 33 µF to 1000 µF) that also limits bass; the bridge cancels the DC level, so none is used and the low-frequency limit is set by the input network and the speaker.

In a bridge amplifier the supply current is a full-wave rectified sine, and each half draws from the supply for half the cycle. Efficiency is low at low output and climbs with power, so internal dissipation is nearly flat across the working range and lower at full power than at half power. At 5 V into 8 Ω a 1.25 W output draws almost 1.8 W from the supply. Efficiency rises as VDD falls.

The highest recommended junction temperature is 125 °C. A thermal shutdown turns the device off above 150 °C junction. At 5 V and full dissipation the 2 mm × 2 mm MicroStar Junior package allows 53.3 °C ambient; at the output levels in the efficiency table no airflow is needed. Speakers above 8 Ω cut the output current and improve the thermal margin.

Use solder-mask-defined lands for the balls: the copper pad is larger than the land and the mask opening sets the land size, which gives tighter size control and better copper adhesion, and the extra copper helps cooling. Put small plated vias near the centre ball B2 into the ground plane as a heatsink. The recommended land carries diameters of 0.38 mm, 0.28 mm and 0.25 mm. Keep the external parts very close to the device to limit noise pickup.

Land pattern: 0.7 mm × 0.38 mm pads on 0.65 mm pitch, 1.95 mm between the first and last pad centres of each row, 3.3 mm across the outer edges of the two rows, a centre pad 1.4 mm wide with five 0.33 mm plugged vias in it, and a 1.4 mm × 1.85 mm solder-mask opening centred on the package. Print paste on the centre pad as a hatch filling 50 % so there is not too much solder under the package.
ESD protection on chip is limited: store with the leads shorted together or in conductive foam to protect the MOS gates.
